title: Premature Attraction of Pollinators to Inaccessible Figs of Ficus altissima: A Search for Ecological and Evolutionary Consequences
screening_reason: Single fresh pollinators were experimentally introduced into monoecious figs on days 1-5 after accessibility; seeds and pollinator offspring were counted in the same figs. Seed production peaked on days 2-3 rather than day 1, giving direct mixed-system interior-peak shape evidence, but group means/uncertainty needed for a formal quadratic effect are not reported in text.
notes: Ficus altissima × Eupristina altissima. Source Poisson GLM across days 1-5: seed beta=-0.09±0.01; pollinator offspring beta=-0.16±0.01; n=27,25,24,23,21. Admit to preregistered H2 shape lane, not strict-H1 slope because the source itself states an interior seed peak.

title: Effect of a Weevil, Rhinocyllus conicus, on Musk Thistle (Carduus thoermeri) Seed Production
screening_reason: The same two-year study sampled four successive weekly flowering cohorts and recorded both weevil incidence per head and fully developed seed production per head; a strict within-season antagonist timing effect should be recoverable if the original week-by-site tables and uncertainty/sample sizes can be recovered.
notes: McCarty & Lamp 1982. Week-1 weevil incidence was 6.7/head in 1978 and 28.0/head in 1979; week-4 incidence was <1/head in both years. Infested sites produced 28% fewer fully developed seeds than the non-infested site in 1978 and 78% fewer in 1979. Abstract-level numbers are insufficient to reconstruct a synchrony effect variance.

title: Seasonal Asynchrony of Italian Thistle, Carduus pycnocephalus, and the Weevil, Rhinocyllus conicus, Introduced for Biological Control in Southern California
screening_reason: Plant flowering extended from mid-April through late August while univoltine weevil oviposition ended in late June; seed loss and realized viable-seed production were measured in the same 30 plants. A before-versus-after-oviposition timing contrast may be recoverable from the full paper, but the accessible abstract lacks the group-specific variance/sample structure required for an effect.
notes: Goeden & Ricker 1985. 7,735 heads on 30 plants; estimated 55% seed loss; 11,410 seeds still produced, mainly after oviposition ended. Do not derive an effect from totals alone.

title: Altered biological control species interactions despite phenological synchrony along an urban–rural temperature gradient
screening_reason: Direct C. nutans and R. conicus phenology and synchrony are quantified across sites, but the response is oviposition/damage rather than a final seed/fitness outcome. The study importantly shows that abundance-based phenological synchrony can stay similar while interaction timing/damage changes.
notes: Central Pennsylvania 2013-2014. Retain as measurement-validity context: adult presence is not necessarily active oviposition, so IWE should prefer interaction/oviposition timing where possible.
